newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries soar as chances for rate hike shrink.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries soar as chances for rate hike shrink.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices were still soaring at midday after weaker-than-expected August retail sales and consumer price data persuaded investors that a Federal Reserve rate hike in September hd become much less less likely.

Early in the trading session, the government reported that the Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.1 percent in August. The so-called core CPI, the index without its food and energy components, was also up only a very slight 0.1 percent. Economists had expected an increase of 0.2 percent.

Retail sales in August were also weak, up just 0.2 percent, providing some evidence -- evidence that so far has been scarce -- that the economy is slowing in the second half of the year. Economists had expected August retail sales to be up 0.7 percent.

"An interest-rate hike in September, which was a virtual foregone conclusion before today, is now dramatically less likely," said John Williams, managing director and chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "Now it's an extremely close call."
On that change in the balance of prospective monetary policy, the Treasury market took flight.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year bond, which was down 5/32 just before the data were reported was up more than a full point within 20 minutes of the data's release.

In early afternoon, the bond touched a session high of 97-18/32, up 1-19/32. Its yield, at 7.07 percent before the data came out, had fallen to 6.95 percent, the lowest since August 23, when the bond yield closed at that level.
Still, economists said the data, while friendly to the bond market, did not tell the whole tale.

"A lot of analysts are standing by their calls that the Fed is going to tighten," said Waldo Best, senior economist at BZT Securities Inc. "People are waiting. They'd like to hear someone from the Fed saying this is good news and they haven't seen it yet."
Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc, said the market "might be overly influenced by the latest data and not keeping in mind what was apparent" just recently.
"We have seen good inflation numbers and slower retail activity but it's important to keep in mind that we have an unemployment rate of 5.1 pct and wages moving up," he said.
"That's an early warning sign of inflation becoming a problem," said Moran.
Williams said clearly the CPI in recent months has shown "remarkably few signs" of any upward pressure on inflation.
But he said the more important issue is whether the economy is slowing -- because inflation lags economic growth.

"We all knew the third quarter would be weaker than the second but we didn't think it would slow fast enough to keep the Fed from moving (rates higher). Now it's possible that the economy has slowed enough to delay the Fed's move yet again," said Williams.
The Treasury yield curve steepened after the data as well.

Three- and six-month bill rates, which were each up one basis point before the data, were down seven basis points and 11 basis points, respectively, to 5.06 percent and 5.15 percent in early afternoon trade.

Two-year notes were up 11/32 to 100-2/32, yielding 6.09 percent. The spread between the two-year note yield and the 30-year bond yield had widened to 85 basis points from 80 basis points at Thursday's close and in early trade on Friday.
Five-year notes were up 25/32 to 100-6/32, yielding 6.45 percent. 10-year notes were up 1-5/32 to 102-1/32, yielding 6.71 percent. -- 212-859-1679
